message.content:
**Hydrogen (H)** – the simplest and most abundant element in the universe – has a rich set of physical, chemical, and nuclear properties. Below is a consolidated overview that covers the most commonly referenced characteristics.

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium), H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) |
| | Standard molar mass | 1.00794 g mol⁻¹ |
| | Standard molar volume (STP, 0 °C, 1 atm) | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| **Physical State (Room Temperature)** | State | Gas |
| | Color | Colorless |
| | Odor | Odorless |
| | Taste | Tasteless |
| | Density (at 0 °C, 1 atm) | 0.08988 g cm⁻³ |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (121 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14 K) |
| | Specific heat (gas, 25 °C) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Heat of vaporization | 0.452 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Speed of sound | ~1,200 m s⁻¹ (in H₂) |
| | Refractive index (visible light) | ~1.000132 |
| | Viscosity (25 °C) | 8.76 × 10⁻⁶ Pa s |
| **Chemical Properties** | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Ionization energy (1st) | 13.598 eV |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV |
| | Standard enthalpy of formation (gas) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition) |
| | Standard Gibbs free energy of formation (gas) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Standard entropy (gas) | 130.68 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Standard molar heat capacity (gas, 298 K) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Reactivity | Highly flammable; reacts with O₂ to form H₂O; forms hydrides with metals; participates in hydrogen bonding in compounds like water and alcohols. |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a weak acid (e.g., H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻) and a weak base (e.g., H₂ ⇌ H⁺ + H⁻). |
| | Spectroscopic features | Strong absorption in the infrared (stretching vibration ~ 3,400 cm⁻¹); Lyman series in UV; Balmer series in visible. |
| **Isotopic Variants** | **Protium (¹H)** | Stable, most abundant (~99.98 %). |
| | **Deuterium (²H)** | Stable, ~0.02 % natural abundance; heavier, lower zero‑point energy; used in NMR, neutron moderation. |
| | **Tritium (³H)** | Radioactive (half‑life 12.32 y); beta emitter; used in radiolabeling and nuclear fusion research. |
| **Nuclear Properties** | Tritium half‑life | 12.32 years |
| | Tritium decay mode | β⁻ decay to helium‑3 |
| | Deuterium nuclear spin | 1 (boson) |
| | Protium nuclear spin | ½ (fermion) |
| **Applications & Significance** | Energy carrier | Hydrogen fuel cells, rocket propellant. |
| | Astrophysics | Primary fuel in stellar nucleosynthesis; H₂ clouds in interstellar medium. |
| | Chemistry | Basis for organic chemistry; key component of water, acids, bases, and many organic molecules. |
| | Materials science | Hydrides used in metal‑hydride batteries; hydrogen embrittlement in steels. |
| | Environmental science | Green hydrogen production via electrolysis of water. |

---

### Quick Reference Highlights

- **Molecular form**: Diatomic (H₂) under normal conditions.
- **Flammability**: Extremely flammable; explosive limits 4 %–75 % in air.
- **Density**: Lowest among gases (≈0.09 g L⁻¹ at STP).
- **Boiling point**: –253 °C; requires cryogenic temperatures to liquefy.
- **Isotopic significance**: Deuterium used in NMR; tritium in nuclear fusion and radiolabeling.
- **Spectroscopy**: Strong IR absorption; Lyman and Balmer series in UV/visible spectra.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
